stances.claim: Rare and few are lawyers elevated to eminent international judicial tribunals -- membership is based on both personal qualities of nominees and the international political clout of the nominating state

Pangalangan was not even a public official -- he was the Inquirer's publisher and UP Law's professorial lecturer/former dean -- yet his personal qualities and the heroic diplomatic effort by Del Rosario's team overcame PH's depleted political quid pro quo clout

Special credit goes to the four Philippine ambassadors -- Ledda (Netherlands), Bataclan (Belgium), Yparraguirre (UN permrep), and Natividad (UN deputy permrep) -- for using Filipino ingenuity, hard work, and battle-tested person-to-person skills

The ICC is a court of last resort available only when national judicial systems fail -- it disregards heads-of-state immunity, recognizes no prescription of crimes or amnesty, and has jurisdiction over genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity, and aggression

The Philippines was unable to get into the ICJ again after Bengzon in 1966 because the Asian region is assigned only three ICJ memberships, two of which are always taken by China and Japan, and the third allocated to the Middle East

CJP records with pride the roster of Filipinos in international judicial tribunals: Bengzon (ICJ), Feliciano (WTO Appellate Tribunal), Romero (ILO Administrative Tribunal) -- and Miriam Defensor-Santiago who was elected ICC judge but had to resign due to ill health

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes a tribute to Dr. Raul C. Pangalangan, newly elected judge of the International Criminal Court, opening with his Friday cocktails-reception hosted in Pangalangan's honor -- with Chief Justice Maria Lourdes P.A. Sereno and DFA Secretary Albert F. Del Rosario as joint guest speakers, representing the judiciary and the diplomatic corps respectively, both exalted by Pangalangan's elevation. Rare and few are lawyers elevated to eminent international judicial tribunals, CJ notes, because membership is based on both personal qualities and the international political clout of the nominating state. Pangalangan was not even a public official at the time -- he was the publisher of the Inquirer and a professorial lecturer and former dean of the UP College of Law (and other universities here and abroad). The ICC requires nominees to possess the qualifications required in their states for the highest judicial offices, plus expertise in criminal law or international law, especially international humanitarian law and IHRL; the ICC selection panel found Pangalangan eminently qualified. The problem was that the Philippines had exhausted its political quid pro quo clout -- but Secretary Del Rosario led PH diplomats in using Filipino ingenuity, hard work, and battle-tested person-to-person skills to make up for the lack of political and financial resources. Special credit goes to Ambassadors Jaime Victor Ledda (Netherlands), Victoria Bataclan (Belgium), Lourdes Yparraguirre (UN permrep), and Irene Susan Natividad (UN deputy permrep). The result was Pangalangan's stunning victory on June 24, 2015, with assumption to office July 13, 2015 through March 10, 2021. CJ then explains the ICC: organized when 120 member-states signed the Rome Statute on July 17, 1998 (effective July 1, 2002); currently 123 members. The Philippines signed on December 28, 2000 and the Senate ratified on April 23, 2011 by a 17-1 vote (Enrile cast the only negative). Unlike national courts, the ICC disregards heads-of-state immunity, recognizes no prescription of crimes and no amnesty, insists on command and individual responsibility, and serves as court of last resort when national systems are unwilling or unable to prosecute genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity, and aggression. On other Filipino international jurists: the only Filipino elected to the ICJ was Cesar Bengzon, in November 1966, three months after his retirement as chief justice -- CJ remembers him fondly because Bengzon signed his 1961 bar membership certificate; Asia is assigned only three ICJ memberships, two always taken by China and Japan, the third allocated to the Middle East. On December 13, 1995, SC Justice Florentino P. Feliciano was elected to the nine-member WTO Appellate Tribunal (and later served as chair). Retired Justice Flerida Ruth P. Romero was the first woman and only Filipino named to the ILO Administrative Tribunal. Senator Miriam Defensor-Santiago was elected an ICC judge a few years ago but was overtaken by ill health before she could discharge her duties and had to resign.
